prompt: In many societies, a growing number of older people live alone and have little regular contact with others. What are the causes of this isolation, and what could be done to reduce it?
essay:
Discussions of loneliness in old age nearly always arrive at the same culprit: families are not what they were, and adult children no longer visit. There is something in this, but it explains less than it seems to. Isolation is reported at high rates in societies with strong family obligation and frequent visiting, which suggests that whatever people are missing, a dutiful Sunday afternoon does not supply it.

What has actually disappeared is the ambient sociability of ordinary life. Most human contact is not scheduled; it accumulates through repetition in shared space — the same bus, the same counter, the same bench. Retirement removes the largest single source of this at once, and the redesign of neighbourhoods around driving has quietly removed most of the remainder. A person who once bought bread daily from someone who knew their name now receives a delivery, and the transaction that was also a conversation has become only a transaction. Nobody decided this, which is part of why it is so hard to reverse.

It follows that arranging visits, however well meant, addresses the wrong quantity. What isolated people lack is not an hour a week of intense attention but the loose, undemanding, repeated contact that makes a person feel part of somewhere. Rebuilding it means treating proximity as infrastructure: local shops and cafés that survive because planning permits them, benches and libraries and covered places to sit, and transport frequent enough that leaving the house does not require a plan.

This is slower and less satisfying than a volunteer scheme, and it cannot be announced at the end of a parliament. It also has an advantage no befriending programme can match. Contact that arises from where somebody lives does not depend on anyone remembering to provide it, and does not stop when the funding does.
title: Loneliness among older people
